title: Frequently asked questions
excerpt: How the calculators work, what the file tools do with your files, and what to do when a result looks wrong.
content:
Answers to the questions that arrive most often — about how the calculators work, how the file tools handle what you give them, and what to do when a result looks wrong. If your question is not here, the contact form reaches a person.

What is Onim, exactly?

A free collection of 4,041 calculators and 19 browser-based file tools, organised into fifteen sections. Calculators are one section. The same catalogue holds the Audio, Video, Image, PDF, Developer, Converter, Security, Gaming, Compressor, Productivity, Design & CSS, Text & Writing, Art & Color and Social & Community tools. Everything is free, and nothing needs an account.

Do the calculators store what I type?

No. The values you enter are used to compute the result in the page and are gone when you leave or reload. There is no database row for your inputs and nothing is attached to you. The same is true of the copy-link feature: the address bar holds the state so you can share a result, not so the server can keep it.

Do the file tools upload my file?

No. The tools read the file with the browser's own file APIs and process it inside the page. There is no upload endpoint for it to reach, which is also why a very large file can be limited by your device's memory rather than by a server limit. If a tool cannot finish the job without sending the file somewhere, the page says so before you start.

Why is one field blank?

Many calculators work out whichever value you leave empty. Fill in the ones you know, leave the one you want, and the result appears. A field is never blank because of an error — an error shows a message under the field instead.

Why does the result differ from another site?

Usually a different assumption rather than a different formula: a different day count in a date calculation, a different rounding step, a calorie that means kilocalorie, a month treated as 30 days rather than a calendar month. Each page states its assumptions. If you can say where the other answer comes from, tell us — sometimes the other site is the one that is wrong, and sometimes the page here needs to offer both conventions.

Can I link to a result?

Yes. The address bar holds the whole form state, so a copied URL opens the page with the same values and the same answer. Nothing about that link is stored on the server.

How accurate is a conversion?

Exact where the unit definition is exact — an inch is 25.4 millimetres, a US gallon is 3.785411784 litres — and rounded where the definition is a convention or the value is measured. Pages that involve a conventional unit say which one they use, and results are shown with at most three decimal places.

Why does a number field refuse letters?

Because a letter in a number field is almost always a mistake that would otherwise produce a silent zero or a wrong answer later. The field says what it expects under the input rather than quietly discarding what you typed.

How do I report a wrong answer?

Use the contact form and include the calculator's name, the values you entered and the answer you expected. A wrong result is a bug and is fixed rather than annotated. If you know the source of the correct answer, say so.

Can I ask for a calculator or a file format?

Yes, and a good share of what is on the site today started as one of those messages. Say what you are trying to work out and what you have in hand — that is more useful than a one-line request.

Who writes and checks the pages?

A small independent team: an editorial lead, an engineering lead and a review lead for the health and science calculators. Some drafting and code review is AI-assisted; every formula, worked example and sign-off is human. The About page introduces the team, and the AI policy states exactly where AI tooling is and is not used.

How is the site paid for?

By advertising: a small number of clearly marked placements, never inside a result and never between you and an answer. Advertisers never see your inputs or your files. There is no subscription, no premium tier and no account.

What data does the site keep?

Very little: ordinary server logs for a short period, the messages you deliberately send, the reviews and likes you deliberately post, and a daily page counter that holds no visitor identifier. The privacy policy is the full list, the cookie policy names every cookie, and your data and your choices explains how to have anything removed.

Can I use a result at work or in a paper?

Yes, with care. Cite the formula the page documents, not the website, and check the result against your own source — a public calculator is not a validated instrument. The disclaimer sets out the limits for money, health, construction and legal figures. Quoting a short passage of explanation with a link back is fine; republishing whole articles is not.

Something is broken or hard to use — where do I say so?

The contact form. Accessibility problems count as bugs here, not as feature requests: if a page is hard to use with a keyboard, a screen reader or a small screen, describe where it breaks and it will be fixed with the same priority as a wrong number.
